items.question: Evaluate the role of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and V.P. Menon in the integration of the princely states, with special reference to Junagadh, Hyderabad and Jammu & Kashmir.
items.modelAnswer:
The integration of the **565 princely states** was, alongside Partition, the gravest challenge to the new nation, and its peaceful resolution is largely credited to **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel** as Home Minister and his Secretary **V.P. Menon** at the **States Department** (1947). With the lapse of British **paramountcy**, each state could accede to India, accede to Pakistan or remain independent — a recipe for 'balkanisation'. Patel combined **persuasion, appeals to patriotism and firm pressure**, offering rulers **privy purses** and using the minimal **Instrument of Accession** (ceding only defence, external affairs and communications) so that accession appeared honourable rather than a surrender. By 15 August 1947 the overwhelming majority had signed.

Three cases proved intractable. In **Junagadh**, a Hindu-majority coastal state, the Nawab acceded to Pakistan; after he fled and administration collapsed, a **plebiscite in February 1948** overwhelmingly endorsed India. In **Hyderabad**, the largest and richest state, the Nizam sought independence while the **Razakars** militia under **Kasim Razvi** unleashed violence; after a Standstill Agreement failed, **Operation Polo (September 1948)**, a swift 'Police Action', secured integration. **Jammu & Kashmir** was handled by Nehru: Maharaja **Hari Singh**, initially seeking independence, signed the **Instrument of Accession on 26 October 1947** when faced with a **tribal invasion** from Pakistan, and the state received special status under **Article 370**.

Patel's achievement — welding a fragmented map into a single Union with remarkably little bloodshed — earned him the title **'Iron Man of India'**, while Menon supplied the administrative craft. The episode laid the territorial foundation on which democratic and later linguistic reorganisation could proceed.
keyPoints: 565 princely states; lapse of paramountcy allowed accession to India/Pakistan or independence — risk of balkanisation.
Patel (Home) + V.P. Menon (States Department); tools = persuasion, privy purses, minimal Instrument of Accession.
Junagadh — Nawab acceded to Pakistan; February 1948 plebiscite favoured India.
Hyderabad — Nizam and Razakars (Kasim Razvi) resisted; Operation Polo, Sept 1948.
Jammu & Kashmir — Hari Singh signed Instrument of Accession on 26 Oct 1947 amid tribal invasion; Article 370.
Patel earned the title 'Iron Man of India'; integration set the base for later reorganisation.

items.question: Trace the evolution of the linguistic reorganisation of states in India up to 1956, highlighting the role of Andhra and the contribution of the Fazl Ali Commission.
items.modelAnswer:
Linguistic reorganisation was one of the defining acts of nation-building in the first decade of the Republic, balancing **regional-cultural aspirations** against fears for **national unity**. The Congress had long promised linguistic provinces, but after Partition the leadership grew cautious. The **Dhar Commission (1948)** rejected language as the basis, favouring administrative convenience, and the **JVP Committee (1948)** — Nehru, Patel and **Pattabhi Sitaramayya** — advised **delaying** linguistic states while conceding the strength of public sentiment.

The decisive push came from **Andhra**. Telugu leaders demanded a separate province from Madras Presidency, and the **fast-unto-death of Potti Sreeramulu**, who died on **15 December 1952**, provoked mass agitation that forced the Centre's hand. **Andhra State was formed on 1 October 1953** with **Kurnool** as capital — the **first state created on a linguistic basis** — igniting similar demands across India.

To manage this, the government appointed the **States Reorganisation Commission (Fazl Ali Commission, 1953)**, with K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru. It **accepted language as a factor but rejected 'one language–one state'**, weighing administrative and national-unity concerns, and recommended **16 states and 3 Union Territories**. Its report underpinned the **States Reorganisation Act, 1956** (with the **7th Constitutional Amendment**), which reorganised India into **14 states and 6 Union Territories** and abolished the Part A/B/C/D scheme. For Andhra, the culmination was the creation of **Andhra Pradesh on 1 November 1956** by merging Andhra State with the Telugu areas of Hyderabad. Later Acts (Maharashtra–Gujarat 1960, Punjab–Haryana 1966, and eventually Telangana in 2014) extended the same logic, confirming that linguistic reorganisation strengthened rather than weakened Indian federalism.
keyPoints: Congress promised linguistic provinces; post-Partition caution via Dhar Commission (rejected language) and JVP Committee (delay).
Potti Sreeramulu's fast-unto-death (died 15 Dec 1952) forced creation of Andhra State on 1 Oct 1953 — first linguistic state, capital Kurnool.
Fazl Ali Commission (SRC, 1953; with Panikkar and Kunzru) accepted language as a factor, rejected 'one language–one state', proposed 16 states + 3 UTs.
States Reorganisation Act 1956 (+ 7th Amendment) created 14 states and 6 UTs and abolished Part A/B/C/D.
Andhra Pradesh formed 1 Nov 1956 by merging Andhra State with Telugu areas of Hyderabad.
Later reorganisation (1960, 1966, 2014) shows linguistic states strengthened Indian federalism.
